Photograph: Chandan Khanna/AFP/Getty Images Florida Winner of Florida python hunting contest nabs 96 snakes: ‘I was on a mission’ Burmese pythons are an invasive species in the Everglades, and the challenge is part of initiative to remove them Lucy Campbell Wed 5 Aug 2026 19.50 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 19.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The winner of this year’s annual Florida Python Challenge hunted down and eliminated 96 invasive Burmese pythons from the Everglades national park, as part of an initiative to remove hundreds of the snakes from the area every year. The challenge invites hunters to participate in 10 days of capturing and humanely euthanizing as many of the invasive snakes as possible across eight designated hunting locations, with the winner taking home a cash prize of $10,000. The event is hosted by Florida fish, wildlife and conservation (FWC), the south Florida water management district, the National Park Service and others. This year’s competition drew 907 participants from 30 US states, as well as Canada and Vietnam. The winner, Tom Rahill, harvested 96 Burmese pythons, all from the Everglades. A python hunter by trade, Rahill founded an organization called SwampApes in Broward county that takes veterans suffering from PTSD on python hunts in Florida’s wetlands. Far-right Republican accused of stiffing student debate champion of $8,000 Read more In comments reported by Naples Daily News , Rahill told an FWC meeting in Panama City on Wednesday: “I was on a mission to get one of our veterans a big snake. I did it. And we wrestled this thing … The veteran was just over the moon.” Once that was achieved, he said he went deeper into the Everglades, where he found the 96 snakes. Over the course of 10 days in July, 280 snakes in total were removed. Before the competition began, 1,400 pythons had been taken out this year. The challenge also awards several other cash prizes, including $1,000 for the longest python killed, which this year went to Rahm Levinson, who hunted a snake measuring 16ft 5in. Burmese pythons are native to south-east Asia, and have wreaked havoc since they were first found in the Everglades ecosystem in the 1990s, consuming resources and wiping out a significant portion of the area’s native wildlife. The apex predators are incredibly hard to detect, contributing to the population ballooning to a number that conservative estimates put in the tens of thousands. Females can lay dozens of eggs, sometimes up to 100 annually, and although many hatchlings do not survive to adulthood, there are fears the pythons are reproducing faster than they can be caught. The annual challenge is therefore now held during the summer hatching season in a bid to boost the number captured. Aimed at raising public awareness of invasive species, and getting the public involved in conservation and efforts to protect the Everglades ecosystem by controlling the number of Burmese pythons, the event has seen more than 1,600 of the snakes removed from the area since 2017. Combined with FWC contractors, who hunt the reptiles year-round, that figure rises to more than 19,000 snakes removed since 2017. Sarah Funck, program coordinator at the FWC, told Wednesday’s meeting that there is no “silver bullet” to solve Florida’s python invasion, but stressed that the elimination of just one python “is a win for Florida’s native wildlife”. Log in here » COUTTS – About 380 kilograms of suspected drugs allegedly declared as bath tissue have been seized at the Alberta-U.S. border. The Canada Border Services Agency says officers apprehended what is believed to be 300 kilograms of methamphetamine and 80 kilograms of cocaine. It says officers stopped a commercial truck at the Coutts border crossing along the border on July 2. Suspected methamphetamine and cocaine seized by the Canada Border Services Agency from a commercial truck at the Coutts port of entry on the Alberta-U.S. border, on July 2, 2026, is shown in this composite of handout photos. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Handout - CBSA (Mandatory Credit) The border agency says the truck was destined for Vilna, a village northeast of Edmonton, with the drugs concealed in moving boxes and a duffel bag. Border officers arrested the driver and the drugs were handed over to the RCMP. The agency says officers in Alberta seized more than 1,300 kilograms of meth and cocaine last year. This report by The Canadian Press was first published July 29, 2026. Skip next section ICE train stops after door opened at 200 km/h 09/02/2026 September 2, 2026 ICE train stops after door opened at 200 km/h The train was traveling from Munich to Dortmund when a door opened [FILE 2024] Image: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty Images A German high-speed Intercity Express (ICE) train was forced to stop near the entrance of a tunnel on Tuesday after a door mysteriously opened during the ride, police said Wednesday. The train had been moving at around 200 km/h (125 mph) and the conductor immediately applied the emergency brakes. There were 238 passengers on board the train, which was heading from Munich to Dortmund. No injuries were reported after police searched the tracks and ruled out the possibility someone could have fallen through the door. The passengers were able to get off the train in the town of Lohr am Main. Germany's Federal Police interviewed the passengers there and took down personal information. The officers also checked to see if any luggage had fallen off the train. The rail line was reopened around 2:30 a.m. According to a railway spokeswoman, there was no technical malfunction with the train. German rail operator Deutsche Bahn declined to comment on whether someone on board the train might have opened the door intentionally. "Doors on the ICE don't just open while the train is moving," according to a brief statement given to Germany's DPA news agency. "The specific cause is being investigated by the authorities," it added. Further details will not be available until the investigation is complete. https://p.dw.com/p/5KHB8 Skip next section IN DEPTH: Germany terminates lease for 'Russian House' in Berlin 09/02/2026 September 2, 2026 IN DEPTH: Germany terminates lease for 'Russian House' in Berlin The massive seven-story building covering an area of almost 30,000 square meters opened in 1984 Image: dts Nachrichtenagentur/IMAGO After Germany on Tuesday said Moscow was behind an attempted drone attack at an airport in Leipzig, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that the contract for the cultural center "Russian House" would be cancelled. The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it has long been the subject of fierce disagreements and a bone of contention in Berlin. According to the Bild tabloid, police said a hand grenade exploded outside a jewelry shop next to the station, causing minor damage to the facade. Police have not immediately confirmed the report of a grenade. Police had completely shut down the station after a bomb sniffing dog uncovered a second "suspicious object," which turned out to be fragments of the grenade, Bild reported. There was no further information available on suspects or a motive. https://p.dw.com/p/5KEVU Skip next section German FM says new EU Russia sanctions coming soon 09/02/2026 September 2, 2026 German FM says new EU Russia sanctions coming soon German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Wednesday said that the European Union is working on imposing more sanctions on Russian individuals in the coming weeks, a day after Germany said Moscow was behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport on August 4. "Russia has escalated and must live with the consequences," Wadephul said at a gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland. "Pressure on Russia is being stepped up and support for Ukraine also remains at ​a high level. That is the unity we are demonstrating at ⁠this ​time," he said, without sharing further details on what the new measures would entail, other than they would target "a large number" of individuals. The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said that the Leipzig incident had "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism." adding that the EU was working on sanctions targeting 1,600 individuals and entities linked to Russia's military industry. Germany's foreign and interior ministers officially held Russia responsible at press conference on Tuesday Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance Officials had discovered a drone between Ukrainian cargo aircraft fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism, triggering speculation over who could have been responsible . On Tuesday, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that although the devices required "a high degree of technical expertise," the plan appears to have been carried out by "low-level" agents. The ministers said the Russian consulate general in Bonn would be closed, along with the termination of the lease for the Russian House, a Russian cultural institution in the heart of Berlin. Russian President Vladimir Putin has rejected Germany's accusations and said the punitive measures are a "serious mistake." https://www.wafb.com/2026/08/22/downtown.text: Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB) - People who work in downtown Baton Rouge have likely stopped into Serop’s Express for lunch. However, customers keep coming back for a reason beyond the food. From strangers to regulars Serop’s owner Luis Torres said he treats everyone who walks through the door the same way. “I don’t care if you’re a janitor or a lawyer. To me, you’re a person, you’re a human being. I love everyone. I love people, you learn something from them everyday,” Torres said. Torres also makes a point of remembering his customers’ names. One customer said, “He knows all of his customers, he’s always happy, and the food is the best you’ll find anywhere in Baton Rouge.” An immigrant’s path to ownership Torres described how he came to own the restaurant. “I moved here at the age of 17 from Belize straight out of high school, and I started working at Serop’s as a dish washer and slowly I was moving my way up – manager, next thing you know I’m a partner then the family sold me this location,” Torres said. A private naturalization ceremony The federal courthouse in Baton Rouge is near Serop’s, and federal judges who ate there regularly asked Torres about his immigration case. In 2017, Torres told one of the judges he had passed his citizenship exam and would be sworn in within two weeks. The judges arranged to move his naturalization ceremony to Baton Rouge and gave him a private ceremony. “It was beautiful, lovely, we had a great time. It was the first time I’ve been to a federal courthouse, and I hope I never go back, you know?” Torres said. More than 300 people attended the ceremony. “You know, I think when you reach out to people – it doesn’t cost anything to be kind to people, man. Just be kind to people. Treat everybody the same. Have that charisma and love for them,” Torres said. Faith and community Torres teaches Sunday school at First Presbyterian Church downtown. “It’s a beautiful feeling, you know? To be an immigrant and to learn to love and appreciate the things that this country has to give, you know? The American dream does exist. It does exist for me. I’m living it everyday,” Torres said. Travel and new cultures Torres said he has a passion for traveling and exploring new cultures. He is scheduled to travel to Budapest. “It’s something that has educated me, you know, to meet all these different cultures, people to drink with the locals as heavy as you can, just enjoy the ride don’t have a plan or agenda, just go,” Torres said. https://www.politico.eu/article/us-greec.text: ATHENS — The U.S. and Greece are launching a new counterterrorism information-sharing program, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday during an official visit to the Greek capital. In a press conference alongside his Greek counterpart Giorgos Gerapetritis, Rubio said Greece was particularly exposed to threats posed by mass migration, human trafficking and different forms of terror. “What we do not wish to see under any circumstances is that the birthplace of the West is threatened by bad decisions, by inaction, and by failure to address challenges,” he said, calling Greece a “strong and model NATO ally” and a “source of stability in an unstable world.” Advertisement Advertisement Gerapetritis said Greece was willing to cooperate with the U.S. and provide maritime assistance in the Strait of Hormuz, ⁠if a viable peace process exists there. Later Wednesday, Rubio will deliver a speech from Pnyx Hill, beneath the Acropolis, one of the most important sites of Athenian democracy. Assistant Secretary for Global Public Affairs Dylan Johnson said Rubio would use the opportunity to call for a “renewal of the Western spirit.” Rubio will describe the shared inheritance of Americans and Europeans as stretching “from Athens and Rome to Christendom to the founding of the American Republic” and warn that Western civilization has forgotten some of its “essential qualities,” Rubio’s aide said. The foreign policy chief stood by U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after U.S. senators and Greek opposition parties expressed concerns over reports that she had ​threatened to use U.S. influence to topple the Greek government. “Suffice it ⁠to ​say, our embassy here is doing a ​great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here,” Rubio said when asked whether Guilfoyle’s conduct is in compliance with State Department ethics.

https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/worl.text: A gravel-road stabilisation test carried out in Estonia in 2015 is being presented by StabilRoad Holding as a decade-long example of increasing material strength. The company said in November 2025 that laboratory tests of core samples taken from the road every two years showed the compressive strength of the stabilised soil had increased by an average of 1.0 to 3.0 MPa over 10 years. However, the companyâs online report does not provide baseline strength values, the number of samples or the testing procedure behind the 10-year comparison. Earlier research commissioned by Estoniaâs Road Administration recorded transverse cracks in the same test area within weeks of stabilisation, as well as further defects during subsequent inspections.The 2015 test on road no. 24109The test was carried out in July 2015 on road no. 24109 KÃµoâKolga-Jaani, between kilometres 17.7 and 19.1, near Kolga-Jaani. A 2017 research report commissioned by the Estonian Road Administration said the road was divided into test sections of about 468 metres. One section used the InfraCrete soil-stabilisation material with cement, while another used M10+50 and LBS polymers with cement. The stabilised layer on the InfraCrete section was 30 cm thick. The report said a 1.5-times surface dressing was applied to half of the stabilised test sections in 2015, while the other half was initially left unsealed so that changes in the stabilised gravel layer could be monitored. The remaining part was repaired and surface-dressed in 2016.âThe current StabilRoad project page describes the Kolga-Jaani project as having been carried out in July 2015. It says the road was later treated with bitumen emulsion and crushed stone in the second year, followed by a 4 cm asphalt layer in the fourth year.Earlier research recorded cracksThe 2017 Skepast&Puhkim report found that the InfraCrete section developed transverse cracks relatively soon after stabilisation. The report said the cracks appeared within about a month. By spring 2016, inspectors recorded 11 transverse cracks up to 5 mm wide, including three on the part that had already received surface dressing. The originally unsealed section also had areas of unevenness and small holes. By June 2017, the section remained drivable, but the originally unsealed portion was more uneven, and the test section still contained small holes and transverse cracks. The same report recorded the InfraCrete sectionâs elastic modulus at 569 MPa in 2015 and 596 MPa in 2016. Its comparison table also gave an average IRI roughness value of 3.06 mm/m for the section. The report also found that 5 tonnes of InfraCrete had been used, twice the planned quantity of 2.5 tonnes. It suggested that the difference may have resulted from a calculation error when the material was spread using a cement spreader.The Skepast&Puhkim report ultimately said the tested InfraCrete and cement stabilisation method was not suitable for constructing dust-free light pavements on low-volume roads when its operating costs and actual test results were taken into account. Its calculated 25-year discounted operating cost for the InfraCrete and cement treatment was â¬116,871 per kilometre, compared with â¬44,451 per kilometre for the surface-dressing alternative considered in the study.What the company says after 10 yearsStabilRoad Holding's November 2025 report presents a different picture of the section's longer-term condition. The company says it monitored the road for 10 years and took core samples every two years to assess changes in the compressive strength of the stabilised soil. According to the company, the strength increased by an average of 1.0 to 3.0 MPa over the decade. The company also says visual inspections found that the appearance of the stabilised road surface had remained unchanged from its original condition. Its project description says the section was surface-treated in the second year and received a 4 cm asphalt layer in the fourth year. StabilRoad further projects that the same level of stability and strength could persist for another 50 to 100 years.The 10-year result therefore comes from the company's own monitoring rather than the earlier Road Administration research programme. The online company report gives the reported increase of 1.0 to 3.0 MPa, but does not publish the baseline compressive-strength measurements, sample count or laboratory testing method needed to independently assess the magnitude of that increase. The earlier research, meanwhile, documents cracking during the first two years of the test. Photograph: Teresa Suárez/AP France Macron bans ‘illegitimate‘ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrest French president will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ regarding demonstrations called for Saturday and after, as part of tough response to recent rioting Angry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting cases Jon Henley in Paris Thu 22 Oct 2026 11.54 EDT Last modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Emmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost of living protests at the weekend. Speaking after a ​meeting with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers, the French president said on Thursday that demonstrations organised by recognised groups would be allowed to go ahead, although their routes could be changed. Protests requested by “individuals or groups with no legitimate authority” would be banned, Macron said. Requests by organisations such as trade unions would be “examined in accordance with the law” but they might have to use alternative routes. The measures were necessary to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, he said, adding: “The rules are simple and I think they’re commonsense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days.” View image in fullscreen Macron attended the security council meeting at the Élysée Palace on Thursday as he sought to restore calm. Photograph: Suarez Teresa/ABACA/Shutterstock Macron blamed much of last weekend’s unrest and looting on rioters who came expressly to loot, but said the worst of the violence was due to “political and seditious acts by ultra far-left groups who aimed to bring down the republic”. “The priority is a return to calm,” he said, adding that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide concrete “next steps” for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards. An initial police ban on a student protest planned in Paris for Thursday was overturned by a court, but marches also scheduled for the day in Grenoble, Rouen, Le Havre and Toulon were halted. Macron accuses Trump and other foreign leaders of ‘stupid comments’ about France unrest Read more Authorities have already declared a ban on “all protests” on Saturday in the centre of Lyon, France’s third-biggest city, where between 200 and 300 shops were ransacked and looted last weekend and the tourist office was set ablaze. Authorities in Marseille, Nice and Toulon announced similar bans for Saturday. In Paris, a march planned for Saturday to be held in the east of the capital, starting at the Place de la Bastille, was authorised but banned from heading into the city centre. However, a separate march through the capital planned for Saturday by students and some members of the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) movement, whose protests over fuel prices rocked France in 2018 and 2019, would not be permitted, authorities in the capital said. Photograph: Giulia Morici/NurPhoto/Shutterstock France’s main student union, UNEF, has also called ‌for rallies on Saturday. Two people have been arrested after Limoges town hall was set on fire. ‘America, this is a warning’: pro- Trump Maga media in a froth over Europe protests Read more The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, was hosting a meeting of key figures from France’s main political parties on Thursday to hear their views and seek cooperation, and was due to meet several big-city mayors later in the day. The tough security response has included partial night-time curfews in parts of several cities including Paris, as well as bans on gatherings in areas such as around the Élysée presidential palace, the parliament and the city’s main train stations. The demonstrations began last month in a high school in Créteil, south-east of Paris, over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings, and spread nationwide, with strikes, blockades and demonstrations by high-school pupils around the country. Those demonstrations have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, six months before next year’s presidential elections, which will choose Macron’s successor.
